content_list.content_text: From 2010 to 2019, technology changed drastically, producing effects we still watch today. Realistic environments, convincing fake animals, actors being aged and even doubled, it seemed there was nothing CGI couldn't do. Who could have imagined that a biopic about Facebook co-founder Mark Zuckerberg could also be a CGI marvel? Armie Hammer (b. 1986) played the twins Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss.

information.contentTitle: Behind the Scenes of the Twins' CGI in The Social Network
information.contentText: Because of the difficulty of finding twin actors who could play the brothers Cameron Winklevoss and Tyler Winklevoss, director David Fincher chose to hire two different actors, Armie Hammer (Cameron) and Josh Pence (Tyler). Since Hammer looked more like the real brothers, the director's choice was to shoot numerous scenes using his face and later apply it through computer graphics onto Tyler's scenes.

content_list.title: This Is What 'The Matrix' Really Looks Like Without CGI!!! - Special Effects Breakdown
content_list.description: Being responsible for the highest-grossing R-rated film of 1999, when it comes to action films, the Wachowskis certainly know how to dream up a masterpiece. But with a big imagination comes the big need to figure out how on earth you're going to make something that isn't physically possible look real.

movie.overview: Set in the 22nd century, The Matrix tells the story of a computer hacker who joins a group of underground insurgents fighting the vast and powerful computers who now rule the earth.
movie.title: The Matrix

content_list.content_text: Actors playing two twin characters is nothing new. Normally, when an actor plays two characters who interact, filmmakers use techniques such as split screens and over-the-shoulder shots, techniques this film did in fact use as well. But more than that, The Social Network (2010), by David Fincher (b. 1962), was the first to use face-swapping technology convincingly. During the scenes, actor Josh Pence (b. 1982) served as a double for Armie Hammer. Hammer's face was then transferred onto Pence's body in post-production. The two would switch who was Cameron and who was Tyler from scene to scene. These techniques paved the way for an entire film about doubles in Us (2019) and for Chris Evans (b. 1981) to fight himself in Avengers: Endgame (2019).

quote.quote: It's awesome. It's like watching a movie, but you're inside it! We were flying! We could be whatever we wanted.
quote.author: JD McCrary, who plays Young Simba in The Lion King (2019)

content_list.title: Mirrors Not So Far from Humanity
content_list.description:
Remaking a classic film is a very difficult thing. There are countless parameters that need to be met and even surpassed. Rupert Wyatt (b. 1972), director of Rise of the Planet of the Apes (2011), knew this and achieved a true feat that left everyone wanting more. Now in Dawn of the Planet of the Apes (2014), with another director, Matt Reeves (b. 1966) has in his hands a doubly complicated mission: to surpass his predecessor and, on top of that, to deliver an excellent sequel.

Picking up where the first film left off, humanity has been ravaged by the simian flu and chaos has set in. The world population has been nearly wiped out and very few survivors remain. There is no more government and the world has become a giant jungle. In the middle of the forest, Caesar (Andy Serkis), together with other apes he freed from captivity, has built something they can call home. They have grown as a family, as a people, and live democratically in a society led with justice and tolerance by Caesar. Communication is done through sign language, which is passed on to all the apes from a young age. This way, they have lived well and in secret for many years, without even sighting other humans. Blue Eyes (Nick Thurston), Caesar's son, goes out fishing in the morning with his friend Ash (Doc Shaw), and when they return they find an unpleasant surprise: a human. Both are quite scared, Blue Eyes calls for help and, at the slightest movement, the human shoots Ash. By then, Koba (Toby Kebbell) has already approached with reinforcements and is ready to attack the human, who is not alone either. The group believes the apes don't understand what they're saying, but Caesar appears to prove otherwise and send them running.

Back on the road, Malcolm (Jason Clarke) informs Dreyfus (Gary Oldman) that the forest is not uninhabited and tells him about the apes. Dreyfus believes it will be easy to get past them, that they are just animals and understand nothing, but Malcolm warns him not to underestimate them. In the apes' home, confusion reigns. Koba believes they should attack while there is still time and speaks about how terrible humans are, showing the scars on his body from the experiments he went through. Caesar believes everything can be resolved if it's on their terms and that there is no need for war, since they could lose friends and the home they managed to build. Together they decide it's time to show the humans that they are not simple apes and that the forest is forbidden territory. What they don't know is that there is a hydroelectric dam very close to where they are, and that is the reason the humans showed up.

Armed and on horseback, they set off for the city to deliver their message. However, the initiative, though laudable, will culminate in big problems and an inevitable confrontation. This film is entirely permeated by a single feeling: tension. The viewer sits almost constantly on the edge of their seat without taking their eyes off the screen for a second. Snacks, popcorn and soda become obsolete. Trips to the bathroom are also out of the question. Matt Reeves managed not only to deliver a sensational sequel, but did better than and surpassed its predecessor, something that happens rather rarely.

Mark Bomback (b. 1971), Rick Jaffa (b. 1956) and Amanda Silver (b. 1963) wrote an excellent screenplay that masterfully illustrates the behavioral similarities between apes and humans. Especially when there is so much hatred and prejudice involved, something that in the film is common to both species. On the human side, Carver (the one who fired the shot, played by Kirk Acevedo) feels anger and blames the apes for having spread the disease that killed countless people. A feeling common to most humans. On the other side, Koba, overtaken by an enormous desire for revenge, believes the apes can and should get the better of the humans while they still have the advantage. And right in the middle of them are Malcolm and Caesar, who believe there is a way to coexist peacefully. Several issues are addressed, but the one that stands out most is the difficulty of accepting and understanding others with all their differences, especially when there are deeper problems. It's much easier to simply point out flaws and mistakes than to put yourself in someone else's place and try to understand. Sometimes reason needs to speak louder than emotion, or impulsive acts end up happening and causing unnecessary friction.

Not only does the plot deserve praise, but also all the graphics, the sets, locations, special effects, cinematography, score and above all the actors who brought the apes to life. If before it was already possible to believe in the emotions conveyed, this time a bond is created between the apes and the viewer, making everything more palpable, more real. Andy Serkis (b. 1964) proves once again that he is the expert in this kind of motion capture technique, but it was Karin Konoval, who plays the orangutan Maurice, who truly captivated me. While Serkis's performance was strong and imposing, Konoval's was tender and of unique subtlety. As for the other actors, all of them played their roles properly, but the highlight belongs to Jason Clarke, who at times reminds me of actor Charlton Heston. And although I'm not a big fan of 3D technology, this time the feature was used well, especially in the forest sections.

Dawn of the Planet of the Apes arrives in theaters to show that it is possible to make quality sequels and remakes, even better than film buffs prefer to believe.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article "Crítica | Planeta dos Macacos: O Confronto", by Luiz Santiago in Plano Crítico

content_list.content_text: This feat also involved the face-replacement technique of Lola Visual Effects, which took what it learned on The Social Network and applied it to the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Before his transformation into Captain America, Steve Rogers is small and scrawny, unlike what actor Chris Evans actually was. In some scenes, actor Leander Deeny (b. 1980) also played the skinny Steve Rogers. In others, the VFX team replaced Deeny's entire head with Evans's head. But for most of these scenes, the visual effects team digitally shrank Evans. To do so, Lola Visual Effects invented a new shrinking method, which it called Steve slimming.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Captain America: Civil War
information.contentText: At the time, Trent Claus, supervisor at Lola VFX, said "Instead of replacing the actor entirely with a digital double, this method allows us to keep the actor's performance and nuances. So we started adjusting Tony's footage on set, through digital compositing", stated the professional from the company that is also responsible for scenes in The Curious Case of Benjamin Button.

content_list.title: Why Jurassic Park’s CGI Still Looks So Good
content_list.description: Today, cosmavoid breaks down why the VFX in Jurassic Park still looks fantastic 25 years later, and why it will probably look just as good 25 years from now.

movie.overview: A wealthy entrepreneur secretly creates a theme park featuring living dinosaurs drawn from prehistoric DNA. Before opening day, he invites a team of experts and his two eager grandchildren to experience the park and help calm anxious investors. However, the park is anything but amusing as the security systems go off-line and the dinosaurs escape.
movie.tagline: An adventure 65 million years in the making.
movie.title: Jurassic Park

cast.name: Brian Smrz
cast.character: Driver of Grant, Sattler & Malcolm's Jeep (uncredited)

content_list.content_text: The artists at Lola Visual Effects said they learned a lot from this experience, highlighting the actor's performance without letting the CGI get in the way. That's a lesson they put into practice when de-aging Samuel L. Jackson (b. 1948) in Captain Marvel (2019).

Besides Chris, Captain America: Civil War (2016) featured Robert Downey Jr. (b. 1965) as a young Tony Stark. Lola Visual Effects once again went into action. Some de-aging cases involve a body double and others involve replacing the actor with a digital double. However, the new technology allowed Downey to perform the scene normally as himself. VFX artists used digital compositing to de-age the actor. That way, Downey could still act in the scene as usual and the VFX team wouldn't lose the actor's many nuances, a technological achievement that helped the team of The Irishman (2019) three years later.

information.contentTitle: Behind the Scenes of the CGI in The Irishman
information.contentText: Although the CGI scheme in The Irishman was effective in making its actors look younger, it couldn't hide that the actors are actually much older, since the de-aging process applies only to the actors' appearance and not to the way they move and speak.

content_list.title: How The First-Ever Moon Landing Was Re-Created In 'First Man' | Movies Insider
content_list.description: Learn how First Man, starring Ryan Gosling and directed by La La Land director Damien Chazelle, used practical effects and CGI to bring Neil Armstrong's journey to the moon to life.

movie.overview: A look at the life of the astronaut, Neil Armstrong, and the legendary space mission that led him to become the first man to walk on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
movie.tagline: One giant leap into the unknown
movie.title: First Man

content_list.content_text: De-aging has become an essential process. The changes can be as big as lifting skin and as subtle as increasing the light reflected off the body. One of the biggest challenges in de-aging a well-known star is that audiences are familiar with how they looked when they were younger, especially with an actor like Downey, who has been in movies since he was a child. So the VFX team analyzed old footage of him – as in Less Than Zero (1987) -, which helps explain why this young version of Tony Stark is so convincing.

quote.quote: "This is not de-aging. This is not face replacement. What you see for Junior [the younger version of Will] is a completely digital creation 100% driven by Will Smith's performance."
quote.author: Bill Westenhofer, visual effects supervisor on Gemini Man (2019)

content_list.content_text: But the de-aging technique wasn't invented this decade. One of its first uses came in X-Men: The Last Stand (2006). But looking at the results from back then to now, we can see how much the technology has evolved.

Besides de-aging, the technology can also age an actor. Hayley Atwell (b. 1982) grew older for a crucial scene in which she plays a much older Peggy Carter. Once again, we have Lola Visual Effects to thank for this transformation.

information.contentTitle: Analysis of the Special Effects in Dawn of the Planet of the Apes
information.contentText: The technique used in the film was and still is widely used in Hollywood in recent years - including the unreleased "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles" - and the 50-year-old British actor is almost an expert on the subject. Serkis has on his résumé important characters created with the help of technology, such as Gollum from "The Lord of the Rings" franchise and the giant gorilla in "King Kong".

content_list.title: 10 Movies That Changed CGI This Decade | Movies Insider
content_list.description: We all know that seeing a movie's behind the scenes seems cool, but what I really want to know is how has CGI changed over the last ten years? Many of these films raise ethical questions - can you just de-age someone? bring a dead actor back to life with technology?

content_list.content_text: Each film is just an excuse for artists to build on the visual effects work done before and improve it. In an interview, the Lola artists said they believe they spent so much time perfecting the neck of an elderly Peggy Carter in Captain America: Civil War that they didn't have much time to work on the actress's face.

Five years later, Captain America would finally get to act his age in Avengers: Endgame (2019), as Chris Evans was aged using a mix of CGI, makeup and a body double. But this time, Evans wore neck prosthetics so the VFX artists could spend even more time perfecting his aged face.

Thanks to motion capture technology, actors could show their full range of emotions while being transformed into basically any kind of creature. Mo-cap, or motion capture, was perfected in the 2000s in The Lord of the Rings trilogy, King Kong (2005) and Avatar (2009). The technique became commonplace during the 2010s, reaching another level in the Planet of the Apes trilogy. Much of the work on all these films was done by the famous visual effects studio Weta Digital. By the time of Rise of the Planet of the Apes (2011), cameras were capable of capturing the subtlest movements and details, which made the apes even more believable.

content_list.title: The Irishman: Much More Than a Mob Movie
content_list.description:
The Irishman (2019) ended up becoming ("unintentionally", in the director's own words) Martin Scorsese's (b. 1942) biggest film. A fiction that follows his Silence (2016), the film is based on a book with a long title (I Heard You Paint Houses: Frank “The Irishman” Sheeran and Closing the Case on Jimmy Hoffa), published in 2004 and written by former prosecutor, investigator and defense attorney Charles Brandt, whose narrative in chronicle form — and it is very important to keep this genre in mind — tells us the story of Frank, a World War II veteran who joins a union and, for more or less simple reasons, ends up becoming a hitman for the Mafia. As the work begins, the character is looking back on his life and his career in the world of organized crime, recounting his connection with the Bufalino family and the disappearance of a famous and admired labor leader who had been his friend for many years.

In this chronicle conceived by Steven Zaillian, who makes an excellent adaptation of the source material, we have a film that unfolds in two dramatic dimensions, each bringing a host of additional meanings to itself. In the first of them, the filmic universe, the saga has at its core three characters developed in the most classical way possible: hard men, children of a time with limits unrecognizable today, before whom we watch life go by and everything change in politics, business, family and… in the very bodies of these men, who at the end of their lives, from the height of their great power — this time we are not dealing with showy or locally important mobsters, as in Goodfellas (1990), for example. We are talking about the sober Mafia, political as well, mostly silent and powerful at the federal level — must deal with their own demons, seek inner peace and truly face the enemy promised since forever: death.

In The Irishman there is silence. The characters don't need to shout all the time. There's no need for music all the time. And Scorsese's direction is so sharp that he manages to build long sequences of tension for each block of the work solely through what we know of these characters, their behavior, what they are capable of and the implications of their actions at the most varied levels of society, all within an intimate frame.

Notice how the director develops Russell Bufalino, the character played by Joe Pesci (b. 1943), who, like his scene partners, is towering in this film (worth noting that Pesci is practically retired and needed convincing and insistence from his longtime friends to join this one more project… thank goodness!). He doesn't need much to convey his menace. He's an old, tired man, sleepy all the time, but whose influence is sublimely captured by the director's camera and thanks to the way the actor embodies his role. In the same vein, there's the class with which Robert De Niro (b. 1943) (Frank Sheeran) takes on this role of an apprentice who gradually gains ground in a territory dominated by Italians. Everything De Niro does here becomes the most organic, most natural thing possible, to the point of making us forget that this is just a character! His lines come out with unbelievable naturalness, and the actor's growth throughout the film is reflected with the same quality in his laugh, in small gestures, in the way he looks at the world and in the way he shows the body's decline. At the other end of the scale we have the new member of the Scorsesean gang, Al Pacino (b. 1940), playing Jimmy Hoffa. His characterization is so captivating and demands so much attention that every line he delivers sounds like a mocking declaration of war that gradually clashes with the strict rules of the rest of the group. What a character!

Looking at the director's immense rigor in guiding the actors and the plot, and in the way he oversaw the editing — which here flows like a river, in one of Thelma Schoonmaker's most brilliant works, managing to make a 3.5-hour film dynamic and hold our attention with the same intensity from beginning to end, which relativizes our perception of time –, we arrive at the other dimension of the work, with The Irishman serving as Scorsese's own analytical look at his career, working with his friends and putting on screen the cinematic signal of an Era… or the end of a kind of film that today's mass audience, for various reasons, no longer wants, no longer appreciates, no longer sees the intrinsic value of. It's almost like going to the 1960s and witnessing the end of the gigantic studio epics such as Ben-Hur (1959) or Cleopatra (1963). Like Silence before it, Scorsese has no longer been finding a connection with today's audience, and neither have other great directors of his generation, resulting in a ridiculously small number of films of this caliber, which rely solely on human relationships, which don't resort to pyrotechnics to hold attention and which take their time to develop an incredible narrative that gives the actors all the room in the world to deliver nuanced, heartwarming performances.

It's ironic that only Netflix — a symbol of the most dynamic society with the most ephemeral interests — went ahead and financed a production like this, at the same time allowing it to reach the public in the most democratic way possible when it comes to streaming, but also "killing" the glamour this kind of work deserves, that is, the VIP treatment of the cinematic experience. And note that the film celebrates (or portrays with a certain melancholy, in the best sense of the term) this thematic/cinematic past through magnificent aesthetic work, with period research that serves the excellent costumes, art direction and even the experiments in cinematography, which is also reflected in the way Scorsese takes the risk of marking time differently on screen. There are no dates in the scenic blocks, only the documentation of each secondary character's death — note the irony — and archival footage or dialogue that indicates the passage of time (mainly) through the Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson and Nixon administrations. And over time, the methods, struggles and attitudes of these characters change, digging an even deeper individual loneliness that grows as they age and forces them to seek things they never thought of seeking.

Perhaps for this reason the great surprise of the work — and disappointment for those more attached to the "agile normality" of today's mass cinema — is the fact that it is in no hurry to deliver fights, to show characters shouting or the many banal and violent deaths we expect from the director's films. Scorsese does what should be done in a watershed for an Era: he doesn't let the habits of the new times interfere with closing the door he wants to close, the door of his own cinema and of his overall vision of the Seventh Art in this decade ending in 2019. The biggest voice here is given to the controversial characters, while the women and other individuals remain in a secondary context, with few or no lines, because this kind of story isn't their story. And if a viewer who has lived at least twenty years watches the film and doesn't understand this treatment given by the filmmaker and the screenwriter, the question remains: what world do you think you're living in?

It is also worth saying that the aging and de-aging work on the characters is something that will certainly generate controversy due to its possible uncanny valley quality, which is to be expected. The point here, made by Scorsese himself, is simple: in 2019, when the film was finished, everything that was possible to do with this kind of technology was done in the film. Personally, I had no problem with any scene in the work using this technology, which is applied heavily in only a few moments, alternating with many scenes where the software complements the actors' excellent makeup (in coloring, elasticity and expression lines), but it's also worth saying that most of the time the makeup is there on its own, without any digital help, and the result is equally spectacular.

In its reflection on life, on the end of an Era, on old age and on the contrast between an individual's hardened essence and the new times around him (note that, in this same crop, Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood (2019) and Dolor y gloria (Pain and Glory, 2019) make exactly the same reflection, in different times and approaches), we finally have the telling of a legend contrasted with its narrator's final fear… and the film about this dilemma, showing the last moments of someone with a grandiose past. This is the The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance (1962) of our Era, with a career review at the twilight of a decade, amid the change in audiences and in the way the Seventh Art is produced, exhibited, understood and discussed. The Irishman is a historic film tailor-made for those who truly love CINEMA. A work that concentrates the essence of Martin Scorsese's work and presents a line of approach that will be better understood, strengthened and relevant as time goes by. In other words, here is a classic.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article "Crítica | O Irlandês", by Luiz Santiago in Plano Crítico

content_list.content_text: Rise of the Planet of the Apes was also the first film to do motion capture on real locations, as opposed to what had been done until then, inside an empty studio. This development would later help them shoot in even more challenging places, such as the Vancouver rainforest in Dawn of the Planet of the Apes (2014), on hot coastal beaches or in the deep snow of War for the Planet of the Apes (2017).

But Caesar wasn't the only great character brought to life by Andy Serkis with motion capture in recent years. Serkis, also responsible for the character Gollum in The Lord of the Rings franchise, played the menacing Supreme Leader Snoke. He appeared as a hologram in Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens (2015) and later in person in Star Wars: The Last Jedi (2017). According to Industrial Light & Magic creative director Ben Morris, they didn't yet have the tools needed to create a realistic Snoke in Star Wars: The Force Awakens. By the time Star Wars: The Last Jedi was released, they were able to add a lot of detail to the skin, such as age spots and veins.

information.contentTitle: Behind the Scenes of the VFX Used in The Jungle Book
information.contentText: In The Jungle Book, the recreation of every tree, leaf and rock was based on more than 100,000 photographs of an Indian jungle, which the production used to build an enormous reference library. That's not counting the 54 species created – with 224 animals. Each frame of "The Jungle Book", which runs 106 minutes, took 19 hours to render.

content_list.title: The Art and Ethics of Digital De-Aging
content_list.description: In the new wave of computer-generated effects, digital de-aging offers instant, painless plastic surgery: pinching, tucking, hiding and erasing the real signs of aging. The technology can create younger versions of our favorite actors, but what for? In this video essay, Leigh Singer questions the increasingly common practice of digital de-aging and its cultural effects.

content_list.content_text: The visual effects team filmed Serkis with high-resolution cameras positioned at every conceivable angle to create a digital clone of him. As Serkis performed, they could automatically capture all of his facial movements, from how he smiled to how he frowned. They even studied elderly people to see how light realistically hit Snoke's skin. The technology developed by ILM in collaboration with Disney Research was used to capture many actors. One of the most prominent: Josh Brolin (b. 1968) as Thanos. Look closely and you'll see every crease, every pore on the skin of the biggest villain in the Avengers franchise.

quote.quote: If he's not in the movie, then we'd have to explain his absence
quote.author: Kiri Hart, Lucasfilm executive and co-producer of Rogue One, on the appearance of Peter Cushing - who died in 1994 - as Tarkin

content_list.content_text: In the live-action remake The Jungle Book (2016), actor Neel Sethi (b. 2003) played Mowgli and was the only human character in the film. He performed on a completely empty soundstage, alongside puppets and creature performers who would then be digitally replaced by the CGI characters. The biggest breakthrough in this film: muscle movement. MPC Film developed new software to animate an animal's muscle structure. Besides the characters, the environments created for The Jungle Book were made entirely in a virtual environment using virtual reality techniques, allowing the filmmakers to step into these environments and place their characters however they wished.

All of MPC Film's work contributed directly to its work on The Lion King (2019). The VFX artists refined their already developed muscle and movement simulations and added more joints and bones under the skin, as a way to make the characters' movements more natural and believable.

information.contentTitle: Behind the Scenes of the Technology Used in The Lion King
information.contentText: Instead of a set, Favreau and company worked in an environment called a volume, a practically empty space occupied only by a platform. There, camera operators used carts known as dollies, just like the ones you can see on any film production. However, they didn't carry traditional cameras, but devices - with the shape and weight of a camera - that, through infrared signals and 3D sensors, reproduce in the virtual environment the work of a real-world camera operator. So, before any shooting, Favreau and cinematographer Caleb Deschanel would enter the virtual Pride Lands and plan how the scene would unfold with the help of controls very similar to those used by Steven Spielberg in Ready Player One. Once the positions of the cameras and other equipment in the virtual environment were defined, the crew and their headsets in the real world went into action and, as they moved across the platform, their camera movements were recreated in Simba's savanna.

content_list.title: Amazing Before & After Hollywood VFX - Avatar
content_list.description: Wait, there were real actors in Avatar? CGI artists are never left to animate characters blindly and, in most cases, they use reference material or even motion-captured tracking points to move the characters precisely as the reference actor moved. In this case, Zoe Saldana's performance was so good that it went unnoticed, entering the virtual world completely in the skilled hands of the CG artists.

content_list.content_text: Rogue One: A Star Wars Story (2016) brought back the Empire's sinister Grand Moff Tarkin. However, actor Peter Cushing died in 1994. So Industrial Light & Magic used CGI to bring him back to life. Another actor, Guy Henry (b. 1960), stood in for Cushing and did his best impression of the Tarkin character. A head-mounted camera rig captured his facial movements. Then ILM used that performance as a guide to digitally recreate Cushing. The whole process took about 18 months to complete. Although Cushing's estate gave its approval, the decision was still controversial. Should you bring an actor back from the dead?

In Blade Runner 2049 (2017), the VFX wizards at MPC Film created a digital double of actress Sean Young (b. 1959) so she could reprise her role as Rachael from Blade Runner (1982). Possibly the most convincing to date. To create the digital Rachael, they 3D-scanned Young and aged her appearance. As with the muscles and joints in The Jungle Book, the most important CGI here is what you don't see: the skull. To create a CGI skull, they combined the 3D scan with work from after Blade Runner. The focus on building this character's skull allowed the artists to build the character's aged features around it. In addition, they focused on the subtleties of Young's face and even on how makeup was done in the 1980s.

information.contentTitle: Behind the Scenes of the Incredible Rachel Scene in Blade Runner 2049
information.contentText: In an interview with the Daily Beast, actress Sean Young admitted she was paid to serve as a model for the digital construction of Rachel in the sequel, but had no substantial involvement in the film. "I didn't have significant involvement in the sequel, I don't know if it was because of my complicated relationship with Ridley. I was just paid to stand still while they scanned my expressions. Honestly, I think the end result looked like sh*t. That's it.", Young said.

content_list.title: How CGI Transformed Animated Storytelling
content_list.description: Just Write explores some of the storytelling conventions that defined classic animated films before demonstrating how CGI forever transformed not only the visuals but also the storytelling in the field of animation.

content_list.content_text: Digital doubles became so realistic that they would eventually allow Will Smith (b. 1968) to act alongside a younger version of himself, while playing both parts, in Gemini Man (2019).

In Martin Scorsese's Mafia epic, Robert De Niro (b. 1943), Al Pacino (b. 1940) and Joe Pesci (b. 1943) were de-aged to play Frank Sheeran, Jimmy Hoffa and Russell Bufalino at various points in their lives. There was no need for the actors to wear helmets, tennis balls or dots on their faces. The tracking marks were invisible. The scenes had to be captured with three cameras at once. Besides the center camera, the two additional witness cameras were infrared, which removed all shadows from a given scene. New software called Flux revealed much more detail in the actors' faces: how their faces are shaded and how light hits them.

For additional reference, the VFX team studied the cast's filmographies. This allowed the actors to focus on their performances and the visual effects artists to focus on the de-aging. But there are some things CGI still can't do: such as making an actor's movements look younger. So a posture coach came to the set to make sure the actors were moving according to their ages for a given scene. Perhaps de-aging an actor's movements will be a CGI breakthrough for the 2020s.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the article "10 movies that changed CGI this decade", by Ian Phillips & Ben Nigh in Insider.

movies.overview: In the 22nd century, a paraplegic Marine is dispatched to the moon Pandora on a unique mission, but becomes torn between following orders and protecting an alien civilization.
movies.title: Avatar

movies.original_title: Rise of the Planet of the Apes

movies.title: Rise of the Planet of the Apes

movies.overview: Pennsylvania, 1956. Frank Sheeran, a war veteran of Irish origin who works as a truck driver, accidentally meets mobster Russell Bufalino. Once Frank becomes his trusted man, Bufalino sends him to Chicago with the task of helping Jimmy Hoffa, a powerful union leader related to organized crime, with whom Frank will maintain a close friendship for nearly twenty years.
movies.title: The Irishman

movies.overview: Following the events of Age of Ultron, the collective governments of the world pass an act designed to regulate all superhuman activity. This polarizes opinion amongst the Avengers, causing two factions to side with Iron Man or Captain America, which causes an epic battle between former allies.
movies.title: Captain America: Civil War

movies.overview: Rey develops her newly discovered abilities with the guidance of Luke Skywalker, who is unsettled by the strength of her powers. Meanwhile, the Resistance prepares to do battle with the First Order.
movies.title: Star Wars: The Last Jedi

movies.overview: Simba idolizes his father, King Mufasa, and takes to heart his own royal destiny. But not everyone in the kingdom celebrates the new cub's arrival. Scar, Mufasa's brother—and former heir to the throne—has plans of his own. The battle for Pride Rock is ravaged with betrayal, tragedy and drama, ultimately resulting in Simba's exile. With help from a curious pair of newfound friends, Simba will have to figure out how to grow up and take back what is rightfully his.
movies.title: The Lion King

movies.overview: Thirty years after the events of the first film, a new blade runner, LAPD Officer K, unearths a long-buried secret that has the potential to plunge what's left of society into chaos. K's discovery leads him on a quest to find Rick Deckard, a former LAPD blade runner who has been missing for 30 years.
movies.title: Blade Runner 2049
